passages.source_text: τοῦ δὲ Πέτρου εἰσιόντος εἰς τὴν Σιδῶνα, πολλοὺς ἐν κλίναις φέροντες πρὸ αὐτοῦ ἐτίθεσαν. ὁ δὲ πρὸς αὐτοὺς ἔφη Μὴ τοίνυν νομίσητε ἐμέ τι δύνασθαι πρὸς ὑμετέραν ἴασιν, ἄνδρα θνητὸν καὶ αὐτὸν πολλοῖς πάθεσιν ὑποπεσεῖν δυνάμενον· ὑφηγεῖσθαι δὲ ὑμῖν τὸν τρόπον δι’ οὗ σωθῆναι δυνήσεσθε οὐ φθονῶ, καὶ αὐτὸς παρὰ τοῦ τῆς ἀληθείας προφήτου μαθὼν τοὺς προωρισμένους τοῦ θεοῦ „πρὸ καταβολῆς κόσμου“ ὁρισμούς, λέγω δὲ ἐπὶ ποίαις κακαῖς πράξεσιν τοὺς ἀνθρώπους ἔταξεν ὑπὸ τοῦ τῆς κακίας ἡγεμόνος κακοῦσθαι, ὁμοίως τε ἐπὶ ποίαις ἀγαθαῖς πράξεσιν ὥρισεν πρότερον πιστεύσαντας αὐτῷ ἰωμένῳ τὰ σώματα σώζεσθαι, ἔπειτα καὶ τὰς ψυχὰς ἐπανορθοῦσθαι πρὸς τὸ ἀνώλεθρον.

ταύτας τοίνυν τάς τε ἀγαθὰς καὶ κακὰς πράξεις εἰδὼς προμηνύω ὑμῖν ὡς ὁδοὺς δύο, ὑποδεικνύων διὰ ποίας μὲν βαδίζοντες ἀπόλλυνται, ποίᾳ δὲ ὁδεύοντες ἀποσώζονται, θεῷ ὁδηγούμενοι. ἡ μὲν οὖν τῶν ἀπολλυμένων ὁδὸς πλατεῖα μὲν καὶ ὁμαλωτάτη, ἀπολλύουσα δὲ ἄνευ του πόνου, ἡ δὲ τῶν σωζομένων στενὴ μὲν καὶ τραχεῖα, σώζουσα δὲ πρὸς τῷ τέλει τοὺς διαπορευθέντας ἐπιπόνως. τούτων δὲ τῶν δύο ὁδῶν προκαθέζεται ἀπιστία καὶ πίστις, καὶ ὁδεύουσιν διὰ μὲν ἀπιστίας οἱ τὰς ἡδονὰς προκρίναντες, δι’ ἃς . . . . οὐδὲ ζητεῖν τὸ συμφέρον οὐ διεφύλαξαν. ἀγνοοῦσιν μέντοι ὡς οὐκ ἀνθρωπίνοις ὅμοια τὰ θεοῦ βουλήματα. πρῶτον μὲν γὰρ οἶδεν τὰ πάντων διανοήματα, καὶ οὐκ ἐν τῷ ἐνχειρῆσαι μόνον, ἀλλὰ καὶ ἐν τῷ ἐννοῆσαι ἕκαστος εὐθύνεται. πολλῷ δὲ ἧττον ἀσεβοῦσιν οἱ ἐγχειροῦντες καλὰ νοεῖν καὶ ἀποτυγχάνοντες τῶν μηδὲ ὅλως ἐγχειρούντων τοῖς καλοῖς. ὅτι αὐτῷ τῷ θεῷ ἔδοξεν τὸν ἐν γνώσει τῶν καλῶν παραπίπτοντα κατὰ λόγον τῶν ἀνθρωπίνων παραπτωμάτων μετρίως κολασθέντα σωθῆναι. οἱ δὲ τὴν ἀρχὴν καὶ τοῦ γνῶναι τὸ κρεῖττον ἐξημεληκότες, κἂν μυρία ἕτερα πράξωσιν καλά, ἐν ᾗ δὲ αὐτὸς ὥρισεν θρησκείᾳ μὴ γένωνται, ἀμελείας ἔγκλημα λαβόντες τῇ μεγίστῃ ἀποσβεσθήσονται κολάσει παντελῶς.

ἡ δὲ ὑπ’ αὐτοῦ ὁρισθεῖσα θρησκεία ἐστὶν αὕτη Τὸ μόνον αὐτὸν σέβειν καὶ τῷ τῆς ἀληθείας μόνῳ πιστεύειν προφήτῃ καὶ „εἰς ἄφεσιν ἁμαρτιῶν“ βαπτισθῆναι καὶ οὕτως διὰ τῆς ἁγνοτάτης βαφῆς ἀναγεννηθῆναι θεῷ διὰ τοῦ σώζοντος ὕδατος, „τραπέζης δαιμόνων“ μὴ μεταλαμβάνειν (λέγω δὲ εἰδωλοθύτων, νεκρῶν, πνικτῶν, θηριαλώτων, αἵματος), μὴ ἀκαθάρτως βιοῦν, ἀπὸ κοίτης γυναικὸς λούεσθαι, αὐτὰς μέντοι καὶ ἄφεδρον φυλάσσειν, πάντας δὲ σωφρονεῖν, εὖ ποιεῖν, μὴ ἀδικεῖν, παρὰ τοῦ πάντα δυναμένου θεοῦ ζωὴν αἰώνιον προσδοκᾶν, εὐχαῖς καὶ δεήσεσιν συνεχέσιν αἰτουμένους αὐτὴν λαβεῖν. τοιαῦτα καὶ ἐν τῇ Σιδῶνι τοῦ Πέτρου παραινοῦντος, ἡμέραις ὀλίγαις πολλῶν κἀκεῖ μετανοησάντων καὶ πιστευσάντων καὶ θεραπευθέντων ἐκκλησίαν συνέστησεν καὶ τῶν συνεπομένων αὐτῷ πρεσβυτέρων τινὰ καταστήσας αὐτοῖς ἐπίσκοπον ἐξῄει τῆς Σιδῶνος.

ὡς δὲ εὐθὺς ἐπέβη τῆς Βηρυτοῦ, σεισμὸς ἐγένετο. καὶ οἱ ὄχλοι προσιόντες τῷ Πέτρῳ Βοήθει, ἔλεγον· πεφοβήμεθα γὰρ (ἔφασαν) μὴ ἄρα ἄρδην πάντες ἀπολώμεθα. τότε ὁ Σίμων τολμήσας ἅμα τῷ Ἀππίωνι καὶ Ἀνουβίωνι καὶ Ἀθηνοδώρῳ καὶ τοῖς λοιποῖς ἑταίροις αὐτοῦ δημοσίᾳ τοῖς ὄχλοις κατὰ τοῦ Πέτρου ἐβόα Φεύγετε, ἄνδρες, τὸν ἄνδρα τοῦτον· μάγος ἐστίν, πιστεύσατε, καὶ τὸν σεισμὸν αὐτὸς ἐποίησεν ἡμῖν καὶ τὰς νόσους ἐκίνησεν αὐτός, ἵνα ὑμᾶς καταπλήξεται ὡς αὐτὸς ὢν θεός. καὶ πολλὰ τοιαῦτα ὡς ὑπὲρ δύναμιν ἀνθρωπίνην δυναμένου τοῦ Πέτρου κατεψεύδοντο οἱ περὶ τὸν Σίμωνα. ἡσυχίαν δὲ αὐτῷ παρασχόντων τῶν ὄχλων ὁ Πέτρος βραχὺ ὑπομειδιάσας καταπληκτικῇ τῇ παρρησίᾳ Ἄνδρες, εἶπεν, ἅπερ οὗτοι λέγουσιν, θεοῦ θέλοντος ποιεῖν δυνατὸς εἶναι ὁμολογῶ, πρὸς δὲ τούτοις ἕτοιμός εἰμι, ἐὰν μὴ πείθησθέ μοι περὶ ὧν λέγω, τὴν πᾶσαν ὑμῶν ἐκβαθρεῦσαι πόλιν.

τῶν δὲ ὄχλων φοβηθέντων καὶ ἑτέρως ποιήσειν ἐπαγγειλαμένων ὅπερ ἂν ὑπ’ αὐτοῦ κελεύωνται, Μηδεὶς ὑμῶν, ἔφη ὁ Πέτρος, μήτε ὁμιλείτω τούτοις τοῖς γόησιν μήτε ἀναμιγνύσθω. οἱ δὲ ὄχλοι ἅμα τῷ ἀκοῦσαι τοῦ κελεύσματος τοῦ συντόμου ξύλα λαβόντες ἐδίωκον αὐτούς, ἕως αὐτοὺς παντελῶς τῆς πόλεως ἐξήλασαν. καὶ εἰσελθόντες οἱ νοσοῦντες αὐτῶν καὶ δαιμονῶντες πρὸς ποσὶν τοῦ Πέτρου ἑαυτοὺς ἐρρίπτουν. ὁ δὲ ταῦτα βλέπων καὶ τὴν κατάπληξιν αὐτῶν ἀναλῦσαι θέλων πρὸς αὐτοὺς ἔφη

context.translation_policy_text:
# Translation Stance

This document states the translation commitments that guide every
decision in the People's Open Bible. Declaring them is an act of
honesty: critics can assess our output against our stated
commitments rather than guessing at hidden biases.

> **Status: first draft.** This document will be refined as the
> project matures. Input and disagreement are welcomed via GitHub
> issues.

## Theological stance

The People's Open Bible does not commit to a specific denominational
or creedal doctrinal stance. Where the source texts presuppose
theological claims — the divinity of Christ, the resurrection,
the personhood of the Holy Spirit, the unity of God — the
translation reflects those claims as the texts present them, not
as imposed commitments of the translator.

Readers from any tradition (Catholic, Eastern Orthodox, Protestant
of any stripe, non-denominational, inquirer) are invited to
evaluate POB against their own framework. Where a translation
decision is influenced by a theological reading — for example,
where a Greek construction is genuinely ambiguous and the English
choice leans one way or the other — that choice is documented in
the verse's `theological_decisions` block and the alternative
rendering is preserved in a footnote.

We do not pick sides on denominational distinctives (Reformed vs.
Arminian, infant vs. believer's baptism, real presence vs.
symbolic, cessationist vs. continuationist, etc.). Those questions
are for the reader and their faith community, not for the
translation.

## Translation philosophy

The People's Open Bible aims at **optimal equivalence**: the most faithful,
intelligible English representation of the source's meaning, wording patterns,
literary form, and rhetorical force. This is not an automatic midpoint between
formal and dynamic translation. Readability serves source fidelity; convention
and familiarity do not override it.

Specifically:

1. **Original-language primacy with reader-conscious wording.** Where
   long-standing English renderings obscure the source text's plain
   sense, we explain the source pressure openly. For *doulos*, the main
   text uses "servant" consistently while notes and the public audit
   trail preserve bonded-status, ownership, and total-allegiance nuance
   where it is historically or theologically salient (Rom 1:1, Phil 1:1).

2. **Translate titles; use conventional name forms.** Christological
   titles are translated to preserve meaning (*Christos* →
   "Messiah" when it functions independently as a title; *Kyrios* →
   "Lord"). In name-like constructions, use the familiar English forms
   "Jesus Christ" and "Christ Jesus." Personal names are otherwise
   transliterated by standard conventions. Thus "Jesus is the Messiah"
   retains the title, while Greek *Iēsous Christos* used as a personal-name
   construction is rendered "Jesus Christ."

3. **Preserve theological tension rather than resolve it.** Where
   the source is genuinely ambiguous on a contested interpretive
   question (e.g., *pistis Christou* — "faith in Christ" vs.
   "faithfulness of Christ"), we render one in the main text and
   preserve the alternative in a footnote, documenting the
   decision in the per-verse YAML.

4. **Consistency of key terms, or documented exception.** A given
   Greek or Hebrew word should receive a consistent English gloss
   across the translation, unless context demands variance — in
   which case the variance is documented per-verse with a
   rationale. The `consistency_lint.py` tool enforces this at
   commit time.

5. **Readable modern English, not archaic or academic.** The
   target reader is a literate 18–35-year-old English speaker.
   Vocabulary should be accessible without flattening theological
   weight. We avoid both ecclesiastical jargon ("propitiation" is
   footnoted, not required) and informality that undersells the
   text's gravity.

## Source distinctions and optimal English

Source fidelity takes priority over mere familiarity or defensibility. A
significant Greek or Hebrew wording pattern must receive an explicit comparison
with the best source-transparent English candidate, even when a prior draft
already discusses it in a footnote. Prior rationale is evidence, not a veto.
Do not infer different meanings from morphology alone or invent theology to
justify different glosses; preserve observable wording without adding claims.
A concise source-qualified or hyphenated rendering is available when ordinary
English otherwise conceals the source pattern. Record unresolved proposals for
maintainer review; do not silently certify them as unchanged or auto-publish.

**Approved scoped rendering:** John 21:15–17 uses **agape-love** for ἀγαπάω
and **phileo-love** for φιλέω, including the repeated question in verse 17.
The ἀγάπη noun's general table entry below is not a rule erasing that verb
pattern. Do not revert this approved POB/SPOB wording to generic “love”.

## Contested terms

The following terms appear frequently and carry heavy theological
weight. Our default rendering and rationale are recorded here.
Per-verse variance is documented in the individual YAML files.

| Greek / Hebrew | Default English | Alternatives considered | Rationale |
|---|---|---|---|
| Χριστός *Christos* | Messiah where independently titular; Christ in the name forms "Jesus Christ" / "Christ Jesus" | Christ, Messiah | Preserves the title's Hebraic messianic meaning while using the recognizable conventional English personal name |
| κύριος *Kyrios* | Lord | LORD, Master | Matches covenantal and NT usage |
| δοῦλος *doulos* | servant | bondservant, slave | Uses reader-facing "servant" consistently; documents bonded-status and ownership nuance in notes/audit metadata |
| πίστις *pistis* | faith | faithfulness, trust | Main text: faith; footnote alternatives where contested |
| δικαιοσύνη *dikaiosynē* | righteousness | justice | Both renderings preserved in footnotes for Pauline passages |
| ἱλαστήριον *hilastērion* | atoning sacrifice | propitiation, mercy seat | Dynamic rendering for accessibility; alternatives footnoted |
| ἀγάπη *agapē* | love | charity (archaic) | Lexical cognates in source kept |
| σάρξ *sarx* | flesh (literal) / sinful nature (metaphorical) | — | Context-dependent; per-verse documented |
| μετανοέω / μετάνοια *metanoeō / metanoia* | reorient / reorientation; toward God where the context warrants making the destination explicit | repent / repentance (traditional); reconsider / change of mind in documented exceptions | See "Reorientation terminology (2026-10-11)" below; do not homogenize regret, divine relenting, or distinct turning words |
| νήφω *nēphō* | clear-minded (most contexts); sober (where Paul explicitly runs the drunk/sober metaphor) | sober-minded | See revision notes in 1 Pet 5:8, 1 Thess 5:6 |
| יְהוָה YHWH | Yahweh | the LORD, Jehovah | Renders the divine name as a name. Where the NT quotes an OT YHWH passage using *Kyrios*, the NT verse retains "Lord" to preserve the Greek; the OT source verse uses "Yahweh". |
| אָדָם *adam* | man / humankind (context) | — | Context-dependent per usage |

## Reorientation terminology (2026-10-11)

Maintainer-approved English POB and SPOB reader wording uses **reorient /
reorientation** in place of the repent family for moral-spiritual redirection.
Use **toward God** when the context warrants making that direction explicit;
use **toward you** in direct prayer, and omit the extra destination when the
sentence already names it, supplies a departure from wrongdoing, or concerns
interpersonal reconsideration. Acts 20:21 explicitly supplies the Godward
phrase. The word *metanoia* by itself does not lexically contain "God."

This is an English editorial policy, not a claim that remorse is irrelevant or
that Greek word parts establish the full meaning. Preserve sorrow, named sins,
faith, forgiveness, and the distinction between a response and its fruit.
Keep separate turning expressions in Acts 3:19 and 26:20. Baptism's relationship
to reorientation must not be rewritten as "only symbolizes" or "causes."

**Context controls exceptions.** Retain regret, relenting, reconsideration,
change of mind, or turning back where that is the supported sense. Do not make
God reorient toward God; do not make a persecutor's demand for apostasy a call
toward God. Preserve contested interpretations in Job 42:6 and Hebrews 12:17.
Extra-canonical authors retain their own conceptual frameworks. Adapting a
historical English witness is not a new ancient-language translation, and must
be disclosed while its source transcription remains untouched.

**No invented intensifiers.** Do not add "fully," "completely," "radically,"
"truly," "wholeheartedly," or a superlative simply to strengthen reorientation.
Preserve such force only where the source supplies it. Hermas V.3.xiii.4
(reader chapter 21:4) has *holotelōs* and *ex holēs kardias*; its existing
"completely" and "from their whole heart" are not new additions.

Traditional terminology remains in alternative notes, original sources, and
historical revision records. Do not rewrite those layers to manufacture a
history of agreement. See [the application report](docs/REORIENTATION_POLICY_2026-10-11.md)
and the hash-bound plan in `config/terminology/`.

## What the translation is not

To prevent misunderstanding:

- **Not a paraphrase.** Every English rendering is tied to a
  specific source-text word or phrase, documented in the per-verse
  YAML.
- **Not a study Bible.** Footnotes document translation decisions,
  not doctrinal application or devotional commentary.
- **Not a denominational product.** The translation is
  intentionally cross-denominational. Contested readings are
  preserved in footnotes, not smoothed away.
- **Not a finalized translation.** Every verse is currently an
  AI-drafted rendering, released openly with full rationale. There
  is no formal scholarly review process at this time.
- **Not a first-century English approximation.** We aim at modern
  English that honors source-language meaning, not at archaism.

## Translating into other languages

The People's Open Bible's long-term intention is to be translated
into every major world language. Scripture belongs to the whole
church; producing POB only in English would contradict the
project's mission.

Each target language is its own translation — drafted directly
from the original-language sources (Hebrew OT, Greek NT, Swete
LXX for the deuterocanonical books) rather than from the English
POB. Translating from English would compound the distance from the
originals and inherit choices that make sense in English but not
elsewhere. Every target language deserves its own encounter with
the Hebrew and Greek.

Each language goes through **several revision passes** before it
is considered stable:

1. **AI-drafted first pass** — a frontier multilingual model
   produces the initial verse-by-verse draft with full per-verse
   provenance, following the same methodology used for English
   (DOCTRINE.md translation philosophy §§1–5, per-verse YAML
   schema, `doctrine_reference` citations where relevant).
2. **AI-reviewer revision** — a second, distinct model reads the
   draft and flags awkward phrasing, dropped nuance, or places
   where the target language's idiom has drifted from the
   source's force. Revisions are discrete commits.
3. **Native-speaker community review** — before a language is
   declared stable, speakers of that language who are also
   familiar with the biblical source languages (or who have
   access to published lexicons in that language) audit the
   text and raise issues publicly.
4. **Public issue window** — a minimum public-review period with
   open GitHub issues before any language moves from "preview"
   to "stable."

**Supported languages will be disclosed publicly based on model
performance and feasibility.** Not every language has an AI model
capable of scholarly-accurate translation yet, and not every
language has a sufficient community of native-speaking reviewers
accessible to the project. We will publish the current supported-
language list, and the ready-but-not-yet-stable list, as we reach
the capability threshold for each. Languages that do not yet meet
the bar are named as such, not silently omitted.

Every language published under this program carries the same
CC-BY 4.0 license, the same per-verse provenance, the same
auditability. There is no tier system across languages — every
supported language gets the full People's Open Bible.

## Change log for this document

Material changes to this document are themselves commits. Prior
versions of the stance are preserved in git history.

- **2026-04-21:** Removed creedal affirmations (Apostles' Creed,
  Nicene Creed, Chalcedonian Definition) and replaced with a
  theological-stance section that declines specific creedal
  commitment. Translation philosophy and contested-terms table
  preserved unchanged; those are methodology, not creedal
  commitment, and the project actually runs on them. Added a
  "Translating into other languages" section stating POB's long-
  term intention to ship in every feasible major language, with
  the full revision pipeline and transparent supported-language
  disclosure. Per-verse YAML citing the old `doctrine_reference`
  values is preserved as historical record; those are not
  retroactively edited.
context.ambiguity_review_standard: Apply the supplied DOCTRINE.md ambiguity policy: a defensible contextual rendering may be used in the main text when material alternatives and the reason for the choice are preserved in notes. A unique or uncontested interpretation is not required. Distinguish (a) an unreadable or unverified source, omitted content, invented restoration, or a construction for which no defensible English can be given, from (b) ordinary lexical, attachment, or referent ambiguity faithfully preserved in English or explained with viable alternatives. The former blocks publication; the latter does not automatically block it. A note cannot excuse unsupported wording: the proposed main rendering must itself be defensible from the supplied Greek. Clearly printed gaps must remain gaps, not be filled by invention. Never change a verdict merely to achieve acceptance.

passages.text: As Peter entered Sidon, people carried many in on beds and laid them before him. But he said to them, “Then do not suppose that I can do anything for your healing, since I am myself a mortal man capable of falling prey to many sufferings. But I do not begrudge showing you the way by which you will be able to be saved, for I myself learned from the prophet of truth the determinations of God, foreordained ‘before the foundation of the world.’ I mean the evil actions for which he appointed human beings to be afflicted by the ruler of wickedness, and likewise the good actions for which he determined that those who first believed in him as he healed the bodies would be saved, and afterward that their souls too would be restored to imperishability.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: Μὴ τοίνυν νομίσητε ἐμέ τι δύνασθαι πρὸς ὑμετέραν ἴασιν
lexical_decisions.chosen: Then do not suppose that I can do anything for your healing
lexical_decisions.rationale: The infinitive construction expresses what the hearers must not suppose; πρὸς ὑμετέραν ἴασιν indicates ability directed toward their healing.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τοὺς προωρισμένους τοῦ θεοῦ „πρὸ καταβολῆς κόσμου“ ὁρισμούς
lexical_decisions.chosen: the determinations of God, foreordained ‘before the foundation of the world’
lexical_decisions.rationale: “Foreordained determinations” preserves the source’s repetition of the ὁρίζω word group rather than replacing it with unrelated English terms.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the evil actions for which
lexical_decisions.rationale: Here ἐπί with the dative introduces the actions or conditions on account of which the stated consequence was appointed.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὥρισεν πρότερον πιστεύσαντας αὐτῷ ἰωμένῳ τὰ σώματα σώζεσθαι, ἔπειτα καὶ τὰς ψυχὰς ἐπανορθοῦσθαι πρὸς τὸ ἀνώλεθρον
lexical_decisions.chosen: he determined that those who first believed in him as he healed the bodies would be saved, and afterward that their souls too would be restored to imperishability
lexical_decisions.rationale: The main rendering takes τὰ σώματα as the object of the immediately preceding ἰωμένῳ. Alternatively, τὰ σώματα may specify the bodily scope of σώζεσθαι: “he determined that, after first believing in him who heals, they should be saved in body, and afterward that their souls too should be restored to imperishability.” That attachment makes the parallel between bodies and souls explicit. The immediate position of τὰ σώματα after ἰωμένῳ supports the chosen attachment, but the alternative remains syntactically viable; αὐτῷ may likewise be represented as “in him” or “him.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: to imperishability
lexical_decisions.rationale: The substantivized adjective denotes the imperishable or indestructible state toward which the souls are restored.

passages.text: Knowing, then, both these good and evil actions, I announce them to you beforehand as two roads, showing you along which one people perish as they walk and along which one they are saved as they travel, guided by God. The road of those who perish is broad and very smooth, but it brings destruction without toil; the road of those who are saved is narrow and rough, but at the end it saves those who have traversed it laboriously. At the head of these two roads sit unbelief and faith. Those who have preferred pleasures travel by way of unbelief; because of those pleasures . . . . they did not even continue to seek what is beneficial. Yet they do not know that God’s purposes are not like human purposes. For first of all, he knows everyone’s thoughts, and each person is held accountable not only for undertaking something but also for intending it. Those who try to think what is good and fail act far less impiously than those who do not attempt good things at all. For God himself saw fit that the person who lapses despite knowing what is good should, after being punished moderately in proportion to human transgressions, be saved. But those who have neglected even to begin to know what is better—even if they do countless other good things—but do not adopt the religious observance he himself prescribed will, having incurred a charge of negligence, be utterly extinguished by the greatest punishment.

lexical_decisions.chosen: At the head of these two roads sit unbelief and faith
lexical_decisions.rationale: προκάθημαι depicts unbelief and faith as positioned before or at the head of their respective roads.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: οὐδὲ ζητεῖν τὸ συμφέρον οὐ διεφύλαξαν
lexical_decisions.chosen: they did not even continue to seek what is beneficial
lexical_decisions.rationale: διαφυλάσσω with the infinitive is understood as maintaining or continuing an activity. The two negatives are treated as emphatic negative concord; a strictly logical double-negative reading is possible in isolation but is contextually less likely, and the preceding printed gap prevents certainty.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: οὐκ ἐν τῷ ἐνχειρῆσαι μόνον, ἀλλὰ καὶ ἐν τῷ ἐννοῆσαι
lexical_decisions.chosen: not only for undertaking something but also for intending it
lexical_decisions.rationale: The contrast extends accountability from beginning an action to conceiving or intending it; “something” and “it” represent the implicit object shared by the two infinitives.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: οἱ ἐγχειροῦντες καλὰ νοεῖν καὶ ἀποτυγχάνοντες
lexical_decisions.chosen: Those who try to think what is good and fail
lexical_decisions.rationale: The rendering preserves νοεῖν as mental activity rather than adding an action not explicitly stated.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: κατὰ λόγον τῶν ἀνθρωπίνων παραπτωμάτων μετρίως κολασθέντα
lexical_decisions.chosen: after being punished moderately in proportion to human transgressions
lexical_decisions.rationale: κατὰ λόγον is attached to the punishment and expresses proportion. It could instead qualify the manner of the person’s lapse, but its proximity to κολασθέντα supports the chosen attachment.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἐν ᾗ δὲ αὐτὸς ὥρισεν θρησκείᾳ μὴ γένωνται
lexical_decisions.chosen: but do not adopt the religious observance he himself prescribed
lexical_decisions.rationale: Literally, they do not “come to be in” the θρησκεία he determined. “Adopt the religious observance” gives that idiom intelligible English without reducing θρησκεία merely to inward belief.

lexical_decisions.chosen: will be utterly extinguished
lexical_decisions.rationale: The verb uses the image of quenching or extinguishing, which is retained rather than generalized to “will be punished” or “will perish.”

source_issues.source_quote: δι’ ἃς . . . . οὐδὲ ζητεῖν τὸ συμφέρον οὐ διεφύλαξαν
source_issues.issue: The four-dot printed gap marks unavailable or omitted wording within the causal statement. It interrupts the syntax and prevents recovery of the clause’s complete content; no restoration has been supplied. The extant words and their double negative admit a defensible contextual rendering, but they cannot recover the missing content.
The article is printed as του without the expected circumflex. This is an accentual feature and does not affect the meaning.
The print has the orthographic form ἐνχειρῆσαι where the assimilated compound spelling ἐγχειρῆσαι is more usual. The supplied form remains intelligible as the aorist infinitive of “undertake.”

passages.text: The religious observance appointed by him is this: to worship him alone; to believe the one prophet of truth; to be baptized “for forgiveness of sins” and thus, through the purest immersion, to be born anew to God through the water that saves; not to partake of “a table of demons” (I mean things sacrificed to idols, animals found dead, strangled animals, animals caught by wild beasts, and blood); not to live in impurity; to bathe after intercourse with a woman, while women themselves must also observe menstrual separation; for everyone to practice self-control, do good, and not act unjustly; and to await eternal life from the all-powerful God, asking through continual prayers and petitions to receive it. As Peter gave such exhortations in Sidon, within a few days many there too reoriented themselves, believed, and were healed. He established a church, appointed one of the elders accompanying him as their overseer, and departed from Sidon.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τῷ τῆς ἀληθείας μόνῳ πιστεύειν προφήτῃ
lexical_decisions.chosen: to believe the one prophet of truth
lexical_decisions.rationale: μόνῳ characterizes the prophet as the sole or one prophet of truth. The phrase could also be rendered “to believe only the prophet of truth,” with the exclusivity attached adverbially to believing.

lexical_decisions.chosen: through the purest immersion
lexical_decisions.rationale: βαφή denotes dipping or immersion and here refers to the preceding baptism; the superlative force of ἁγνοτάτης is retained.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἀναγεννηθῆναι θεῷ διὰ τοῦ σώζοντος ὕδατος
lexical_decisions.chosen: to be born anew to God through the water that saves
lexical_decisions.rationale: The rendering preserves both the God-directed dative θεῷ and the source’s direct description of the water as saving.

lexical_decisions.chosen: animals found dead, strangled animals, animals caught by wild beasts
lexical_decisions.rationale: These substantivized plurals occur in a list of prohibited foods. “Animals found dead” expresses νεκρῶν contextually; more literally it is simply “dead things.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: to bathe after intercourse with a woman
lexical_decisions.rationale: κοίτη γυναικός literally refers to a woman’s bed but in this purity context denotes sexual intercourse.

lexical_decisions.chosen: while women themselves must also observe menstrual separation
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἄφεδρος is a term for menstruation or the associated period of separation. The phrase may also be rendered “observe the menstrual period”; the source does not explicitly repeat the preceding command to bathe.

lexical_decisions.chosen: reoriented themselves
lexical_decisions.rationale: The context describes moral and religious redirection accompanying belief; the traditional alternative is “repented.” No Godward phrase is added because the Greek does not state one here.

lexical_decisions.chosen: overseer
lexical_decisions.rationale: The word designates the supervisory office assigned to the elder; “bishop” is a possible institutional rendering but may imply a later fixed title.

passages.text: As soon as he set foot in Berytus, an earthquake occurred. The crowds approached Peter and said, “Help us! For we are afraid,” they declared, “that perhaps we may all be utterly destroyed.” Then Simon, taking courage, together with Appion, Anubion, Athenodorus, and the rest of his companions, publicly shouted to the crowds against Peter: “Flee from this man, men! He is a magician—believe it! He himself brought the earthquake upon us and stirred up the diseases, so that he might overawe you as though he himself were a god.” Simon’s party made many such false claims against Peter, alleging that he possessed power beyond human capacity. But when the crowds fell silent for him, Peter gave a slight smile and said with startling boldness, “Men, I acknowledge that, if God wills, I am able to do the very things these men say. What is more, if you do not heed me in what I say, I am ready to tear your entire city up from its foundations.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: set foot in Berytus
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἐπιβαίνω with the genitive can denote entering or setting foot in a place; “Berytus” preserves the ancient city name rather than modernizing it to Beirut.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: καὶ τὸν σεισμὸν αὐτὸς ἐποίησεν ἡμῖν
lexical_decisions.chosen: He himself brought the earthquake upon us
lexical_decisions.rationale: The dative ἡμῖν presents the earthquake as something caused for or against the speakers; “upon us” conveys the hostile result.

lexical_decisions.chosen: so that he might overawe you
lexical_decisions.rationale: καταπλήσσω can denote terrifying, stunning, or overwhelming with amazement. “Overawe” fits the accusation that Peter is using wonders to induce a false perception of divinity.

lexical_decisions.chosen: as though he himself were a god
lexical_decisions.rationale: The anarthrous predicate θεός permits “a god,” while “God” is also possible in the work’s monotheistic setting. The chosen wording preserves the accusers’ comparison without identifying Peter with the supreme God unambiguously.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὡς ὑπὲρ δύναμιν ἀνθρωπίνην δυναμένου τοῦ Πέτρου
lexical_decisions.chosen: alleging that he possessed power beyond human capacity
lexical_decisions.rationale: The ὡς construction presents this superhuman ability as the content or guise of Simon’s party’s false allegations.

lexical_decisions.chosen: with startling boldness
lexical_decisions.rationale: παρρησία denotes open, confident speech, while καταπληκτική marks its astonishing or overwhelming effect.

lexical_decisions.chosen: to tear your entire city up from its foundations
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἐκβαθρεύω evokes uprooting or razing down to the foundations, an image stronger than simply “destroy.”

source_issues.issue: The purpose clause is printed with the future indicative καταπλήξεται after ἵνα rather than the more classically expected subjunctive. Such use is defensible as later Greek syntax, and the supplied reading clearly supports a purpose clause without emendation.

passages.text: When the crowds became frightened and promised to act otherwise as they might be commanded by him, Peter said, “None of you is to associate with these sorcerers or mingle with them.” As soon as the crowds heard the brief command, they picked up sticks and pursued them until they had driven them completely out of the city. Then the sick and demon-possessed among them came in and threw themselves at Peter’s feet. But when he saw this and wished to dispel their consternation, he said to them:

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἑτέρως ποιήσειν ἐπαγγειλαμένων ὅπερ ἂν ὑπ’ αὐτοῦ κελεύωνται
lexical_decisions.chosen: promised to act otherwise as they might be commanded by him
lexical_decisions.rationale: The supplied ἑτέρως is taken in its normal sense, “differently” or “otherwise,” indicating a promised change of conduct in accordance with Peter’s commands.

lexical_decisions.chosen: with these sorcerers
lexical_decisions.rationale: γόης can denote a sorcerer, charlatan, or impostor. “Sorcerers” fits the immediately preceding accusation of magic, though “charlatans” remains possible.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the brief command
lexical_decisions.rationale: σύντομος characterizes the command as concise or terse; “brief” preserves its form without adding an emotional tone.

lexical_decisions.chosen: they picked up sticks
lexical_decisions.rationale: ξύλα literally denotes pieces of wood; in the pursuit scene, “sticks” expresses their likely use without specifying weapons more precisely than the source.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the sick and demon-possessed among them
lexical_decisions.rationale: αὐτῶν most naturally refers to the crowds, though grammatically it could be heard as a possessive “their.” “Among them” avoids implying that the crowds owned or controlled the afflicted people.

lexical_decisions.chosen: to dispel their consternation
lexical_decisions.rationale: κατάπληξις can be amazement, shock, or terror. In the aftermath of Peter’s threat and the people’s prostration, “consternation” preserves both alarm and astonishment.

source_issues.source_quote: ἑτέρως ποιήσειν ἐπαγγειλαμένων ὅπερ ἂν ὑπ’ αὐτοῦ κελεύωνται
source_issues.issue: The adverb ἑτέρως (“differently”) produces a compressed connection with the following relative clause, but it can defensibly mean that the crowds promised to change their conduct in conformity with his commands. The smoother ἑτοίμως (“readily”) is a possible conjecture only and has not been used in the translation.
source_issues.proposed_reading: ἑτοίμως ποιήσειν ἐπαγγειλαμένων ὅπερ ἂν ὑπ’ αὐτοῦ κελεύωνται

Translation Stance

This document states the translation commitments that guide every
decision in the People's Open Bible. Declaring them is an act of
honesty: critics can assess our output against our stated
commitments rather than guessing at hidden biases.

> **Status: first draft.** This document will be refined as the
> project matures. Input and disagreement are welcomed via GitHub
> issues.

## Theological stance

The People's Open Bible does not commit to a specific denominational
or creedal doctrinal stance. Where the source texts presuppose
theological claims — the divinity of Christ, the resurrection,
the personhood of the Holy Spirit, the unity of God — the
translation reflects those claims as the texts present them, not
as imposed commitments of the translator.

Readers from any tradition (Catholic, Eastern Orthodox, Protestant
of any stripe, non-denominational, inquirer) are invited to
evaluate POB against their own framework. Where a translation
decision is influenced by a theological reading — for example,
where a Greek construction is genuinely ambiguous and the English
choice leans one way or the other — that choice is documented in
the verse's `theological_decisions` block and the alternative
rendering is preserved in a footnote.

We do not pick sides on denominational distinctives (Reformed vs.
Arminian, infant vs. believer's baptism, real presence vs.
symbolic, cessationist vs. continuationist, etc.). Those questions
are for the reader and their faith community, not for the
translation.

## Translation philosophy

The People's Open Bible aims at **optimal equivalence**: the most faithful,
intelligible English representation of the source's meaning, wording patterns,
literary form, and rhetorical force. This is not an automatic midpoint between
formal and dynamic translation. Readability serves source fidelity; convention
and familiarity do not override it.

Specifically:

1. **Original-language primacy with reader-conscious wording.** Where
   long-standing English renderings obscure the source text's plain
   sense, we explain the source pressure openly. For *doulos*, the main
   text uses "servant" consistently while notes and the public audit
   trail preserve bonded-status, ownership, and total-allegiance nuance
   where it is historically or theologically salient (Rom 1:1, Phil 1:1).

2. **Translate titles; use conventional name forms.** Christological
   titles are translated to preserve meaning (*Christos* →
   "Messiah" when it functions independently as a title; *Kyrios* →
   "Lord"). In name-like constructions, use the familiar English forms
   "Jesus Christ" and "Christ Jesus." Personal names are otherwise
   transliterated by standard conventions. Thus "Jesus is the Messiah"
   retains the title, while Greek *Iēsous Christos* used as a personal-name
   construction is rendered "Jesus Christ."

3. **Preserve theological tension rather than resolve it.** Where
   the source is genuinely ambiguous on a contested interpretive
   question (e.g., *pistis Christou* — "faith in Christ" vs.
   "faithfulness of Christ"), we render one in the main text and
   preserve the alternative in a footnote, documenting the
   decision in the per-verse YAML.

4. **Consistency of key terms, or documented exception.** A given
   Greek or Hebrew word should receive a consistent English gloss
   across the translation, unless context demands variance — in
   which case the variance is documented per-verse with a
   rationale. The `consistency_lint.py` tool enforces this at
   commit time.

5. **Readable modern English, not archaic or academic.** The
   target reader is a literate 18–35-year-old English speaker.
   Vocabulary should be accessible without flattening theological
   weight. We avoid both ecclesiastical jargon ("propitiation" is
   footnoted, not required) and informality that undersells the
   text's gravity.

## Source distinctions and optimal English

Source fidelity takes priority over mere familiarity or defensibility. A
significant Greek or Hebrew wording pattern must receive an explicit comparison
with the best source-transparent English candidate, even when a prior draft
already discusses it in a footnote. Prior rationale is evidence, not a veto.
Do not infer different meanings from morphology alone or invent theology to
justify different glosses; preserve observable wording without adding claims.
A concise source-qualified or hyphenated rendering is available when ordinary
English otherwise conceals the source pattern. Record unresolved proposals for

## Reorientation terminology (2026-10-11)

Maintainer-approved English POB and SPOB reader wording uses **reorient /
reorientation** in place of the repent family for moral-spiritual redirection.
Use **toward God** when the context warrants making that direction explicit;
use **toward you** in direct prayer, and omit the extra destination when the
sentence already names it, supplies a departure from wrongdoing, or concerns
interpersonal reconsideration. Acts 20:21 explicitly supplies the Godward
phrase. The word *metanoia* by itself does not lexically contain "God."

This is an English editorial policy, not a claim that remorse is irrelevant or
that Greek word parts establish the full meaning. Preserve sorrow, named sins,
faith, forgiveness, and the distinction between a response and its fruit.
Keep separate turning expressions in Acts 3:19 and 26:20. Baptism's relationship
to reorientation must not be rewritten as "only symbolizes" or "causes."

**Context controls exceptions.** Retain regret, relenting, reconsideration,
change of mind, or turning back where that is the supported sense. Do not make
God reorient toward God; do not make a persecutor's demand for apostasy a call
toward God. Preserve contested interpretations in Job 42:6 and Hebrews 12:17.
Extra-canonical authors retain their own conceptual frameworks. Adapting a
historical English witness is not a new ancient-language translation, and must
be disclosed while its source transcription remains untouched.

**No invented intensifiers.** Do not add "fully," "completely," "radically,"
"truly," "wholeheartedly," or a superlative simply to strengthen reorientation.
Preserve such force only where the source supplies it. Hermas V.3.xiii.4
(reader chapter 21:4) has *holotelōs* and *ex holēs kardias*; its existing
"completely" and "from their whole heart" are not new additions.

Traditional terminology remains in alternative notes, original sources, and
historical revision records. Do not rewrite those layers to manufacture a
history of agreement. See [the application report](docs/REORIENTATION_POLICY_2026-10-11.md)
and the hash-bound plan in `config/terminology/`.

## What the translation is not

To prevent misunderstanding:

- **Not a paraphrase.** Every English rendering is tied to a
  specific source-text word or phrase, documented in the per-verse
  YAML.
- **Not a study Bible.** Footnotes document translation decisions,
  not doctrinal application or devotional commentary.
- **Not a denominational product.** The translation is
  intentionally cross-denominational. Contested readings are
  preserved in footnotes, not smoothed away.
- **Not a finalized translation.** Every verse is currently an
  AI-drafted rendering, released openly with full rationale. There
  is no formal scholarly review process at this time.
- **Not a first-century English approximation.** We aim at modern
  English that honors source-language meaning, not at archaism.

## Translating into other languages

The People's Open Bible's long-term intention is to be translated
into every major world language. Scripture belongs to the whole
church; producing POB only in English would contradict the
project's mission.

Each target language is its own translation — drafted directly
from the original-language sources (Hebrew OT, Greek NT, Swete
LXX for the deuterocanonical books) rather than from the English
POB. Translating from English would compound the distance from the
originals and inherit choices that make sense in English but not
elsewhere. Every target language deserves its own encounter with
the Hebrew and Greek.

Each language goes through **several revision passes** before it
is considered stable:

1. **AI-drafted first pass** — a frontier multilingual model
   produces the initial verse-by-verse draft with full per-verse
   provenance, following the same methodology used for English
   (DOCTRINE.md translation philosophy §§1–5, per-verse YAML
   schema, `doctrine_reference` citations where relevant).
2. **AI-reviewer revision** — a second, distinct model reads the
   draft and flags awkward phrasing, dropped nuance, or places
   where the target language's idiom has drifted from the
   source's force. Revisions are discrete commits.
3. **Native-speaker community review** — before a language is
   declared stable, speakers of that language who are also
   familiar with the biblical source languages (or who have
   access to published lexicons in that language) audit the
   text and raise issues publicly.
4. **Public issue window** — a minimum public-review period with
   open GitHub issues before any language moves from "preview"
   to "stable."

**Supported languages will be disclosed publicly based on model
performance and feasibility.** Not every language has an AI model
capable of scholarly-accurate translation yet, and not every
language has a sufficient community of native-speaking reviewers
accessible to the project. We will publish the current supported-
language list, and the ready-but-not-yet-stable list, as we reach
the capability threshold for each. Languages that do not yet meet
the bar are named as such, not silently omitted.

Every language published under this program carries the same
CC-BY 4.0 license, the same per-verse provenance, the same
auditability. There is no tier system across languages — every
supported language gets the full People's Open Bible.
